content: Nutrition counseling and education, whether provided individually or in groups, play a critical role in helping individuals manage or modify their food choices and eating behaviors. Establishing linkages and two-way referrals between health clinics and community-level services, such as TB or HIV support groups and mother-to-mother support groups, is recommended. Socioeconomic and gender-related barriers to accessing care, such as unsuitable clinic hours for working individuals or childcare responsibilities disproportionately affecting women, should be identified and addressed to improve adherence to clinical and community services. Nutritional support for undernourished individuals with TB should align with the support provided to others with similar nutritional statuses, regardless of TB status. This support should be facilitated through referrals to available nutritional services. Many adults may struggle to consume large amounts of ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF); therefore, combining RUTF with fortified blended foods (FBF) and improving access to locally nutritious foods through cash or voucher assistance is often recommended. Households affected by TB should undergo socioeconomic assessments to determine eligibility for additional support, regardless of their nutritional status. This support may include in-kind or cash assistance, linkage to social protection initiatives, and time-limited aid until health improves and income-generating activities can resume. Community-level economic strengthening and livelihood services, such as microfinance and vocational training, should also be provided to enhance food security. Nutrition assessment, counseling, and support should be integrated for optimal health and nutrition outcomes, as each component alone is insufficient. TB patients should also be screened and treated for common comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus, mental health disorders, and substance use disorders, as part of a comprehensive care package. Early diagnosis and management of these conditions are crucial for successful TB treatment completion and cure. The recommended approach for smoking cessation includes asking about smoking status, providing brief personalized advice, and arranging cessation support. In humanitarian emergencies, TB services must continue uninterrupted, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. The TB workforce should be trained to address emerging infectious diseases and assist with infection control, active case finding, and contact tracing. Simultaneous testing for TB and other diseases with similar clinical presentations, such as COVID-19, can reduce diagnostic delays. TB treatment should not be delayed unless drug-drug interactions are anticipated.
